slides.text:
Welcome to Module 5, Reasoning with SQL Logic.

[pause=0.7]

In the previous module, we focused on summarizing data. In this module, we are going to focus on decision making. In other words, how can we tell SQL exactly which records we want, how different conditions should work together, and what should happen when information is missing?

We will work with AND, OR, and NOT. We will also look at TRUE, FALSE, and UNKNOWN, because SQL does not always work with only two logical states. Later, we will use tools such as coalesce, null if, and case expressions to build more realistic business rules.

As you move through this module, do not just memorize the syntax. Try to read each SQL condition as a sentence. Ask yourself, what rule am I actually giving to the database?

[pause=1.0]

Before we start writing code, I want to connect this module to what we already learned.

[pause=0.7]

In Module 4, we summarized rows. We counted records, calculated averages, grouped data, and created analytical summaries.

Module 5 is different. Now we are asking SQL to make decisions about individual values and records.

For example, should this patient be included in a report? Is this billing record considered high value? Does this patient have a usable contact method? What should happen when a value is missing?

A good habit is to first explain the rule in normal language. Then break that rule into smaller conditions. After that, translate those conditions into SQL.

We will also test edge cases, because a query can run successfully and still give the wrong answer.

[pause=1.0]

Here is what we are going to learn in this module.

[pause=0.7]

First, we will combine conditions using AND, OR, and NOT.

[pause=0.4]

Next, we will discuss three-valued logic. This is important because SQL conditions can evaluate to TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN.

[pause=0.4]

Then we will work with missing values and learn why null needs special treatment.

We will also use case expressions to convert business rules into categories and labels.

[pause=0.5]

Finally, we will combine these ideas in realistic examples and exercises.

As you work through the module, focus on understanding what each condition means. If you can explain the logic clearly in plain language, writing the SQL becomes much easier.

[pause=1.0]

This slide gives us a simple workflow for building SQL logic.

[pause=0.7]

Step one is to define the rule in plain language. Do not start with SQL yet.

[pause=0.4]

Step two is to inspect the fields involved and ask whether any of them can contain null values.

[pause=0.4]

Step three is to group related conditions. This is where parentheses become very important.

[pause=0.4]

Step four is to decide the order of your case conditions. Remember that the first matching case branch wins.

[pause=0.4]

Step five is to test unusual records, including null values, blank text, zero values, and exact boundaries.

[pause=0.7]

Finally, validate the result against the original rule.

The main idea is simple: reason first, then write the SQL. A clear rule usually leads to clearer code.

[pause=1.0]

Throughout this module, we will use a small synthetic healthcare-style dataset.

[pause=0.7]

We have a patient information table with demographic and contact fields. We have a diagnostics table, a patient billing table, and an admissions table.

We also have a convenience view called patient case. This view brings several useful fields together so we can focus on SQL logic without spending all of our time writing joins.

The data is synthetic, so it is safe to use for practice.

When we reach a slide with executable SQL, you can run the code directly here in the browser. You can also use the Copy button, open the Query Tool in pgAdmin, paste the query, and run it in PostgreSQL there.

Using both approaches is good practice.

[pause=1.0]

Three operators are at the center of most SQL decision rules: AND, OR, and NOT.

[pause=0.7]

AND means that all connected conditions need to be true.

OR means that at least one of the connected conditions needs to be true.

NOT reverses a known logical condition.

A simple way to remember this is that AND usually makes a result more restrictive, while OR usually makes it broader.

But there is one important detail. SQL has a third logical state called UNKNOWN. This normally appears when null values are involved.

So as we work through these examples, do not assume every condition is simply true or false. Sometimes SQL does not have enough information to make that decision.

[pause=1.0]

Now let's start with AND.

[pause=0.7]

AND means every connected condition must be satisfied.

Here, our rule says that the patient must be active, the age must be greater than or equal to forty, and the severity must be High.

Notice how each additional AND condition makes the result more restrictive.

[pause=0.8]

Below the explanation, we have a SQL code cell. You can click Run and execute this query directly in the browser. After it runs, look at the result and check whether every returned row satisfies all three conditions.

[pause=0.5]

You can also click Copy, open pgAdmin, paste the query into the Query Tool, and run exactly the same SQL there.

When reading the WHERE clause, say it as a sentence: keep records where the patient is active, and age is at least forty, and severity is High.

[pause=1.0]

Now let's compare AND with OR.

[pause=0.7]

OR means that a record can satisfy any one of several alternatives.

In this example, we want patients whose diagnosis is Pneumonia, Flu, or Asthma.

Because these are alternatives, OR makes sense.

[pause=0.8]

We have a runnable SQL example at the bottom of the slide. Try running it in the browser and look at the diagnosis column in the result. Each returned row should match at least one of the three diagnoses.

[pause=0.5]

If you are practicing with pgAdmin, use the Copy button and paste the query into the Query Tool.

Later, when several alternatives all apply to the same column, we can often make the query shorter with an IN condition. But first, it is useful to understand exactly what the OR statements are doing.

[pause=1.0]

Next we have NOT.

[pause=0.7]

NOT is used when we want to exclude a condition.

In this example, we keep active patients, but we exclude two diagnoses.

Notice the parentheses around the diagnosis condition. They make it very clear which part of the logic we are reversing.

[pause=0.8]

The query is available in the SQL box. Run it here in the browser first. Look at the results and confirm that the excluded diagnoses do not appear.

[pause=0.5]

You can also copy the query into pgAdmin and run it against the same practice tables.

One important point is that NOT does not magically solve missing values. If a condition is UNKNOWN because of null, applying NOT still leaves it UNKNOWN. We will see why that matters in a few slides.

[pause=1.0]

When AND, OR, and NOT appear together, SQL follows an order of operations.

[pause=0.7]

NOT is evaluated first, then AND, and then OR.

This is similar to the idea of order of operations in mathematics.

The problem is that a query can be technically correct but still be difficult for another person to read.

That is why I recommend using parentheses whenever AND and OR are mixed in the same rule.

Parentheses are not only for the database. They are also documentation for you and for anyone else reading the query later.

If your business rule says that two conditions belong together, show that relationship explicitly with parentheses.

[pause=1.0]

This slide is very important because the two conditions look similar, but they do not mean the same thing.

[pause=0.7]

In the first version, SQL evaluates the AND portion before the OR portion. This means the consent requirement does not necessarily apply to every patient selected by the age condition.

In the second version, we put age or diagnosis inside parentheses, and then require consent for the entire group.

[pause=0.8]

You have both versions in the code cell.

[pause=0.7]

Before you click Run, make a prediction. Which patient might appear in the first result but disappear in the second?

[pause=0.4]

Then run the code in the browser and compare the outputs.

You can also copy both queries into pgAdmin and run them one at a time.

This is a good example of why parentheses are part of the meaning of the rule, not just formatting.

[pause=1.0]

SQL logic has three possible results: TRUE, FALSE, and UNKNOWN.

[pause=0.7]

TRUE means the condition is satisfied.

FALSE means the condition is not satisfied.

UNKNOWN means SQL does not have enough information to determine whether the condition is true or false.

This usually happens because a null value is involved.

[pause=0.7]

The most important rule on this slide is about the WHERE clause.

A WHERE clause keeps only rows where the condition evaluates to TRUE.

Rows that evaluate to FALSE are removed, but rows that evaluate to UNKNOWN are also removed.

That behavior explains many surprising results when we start working with missing data.

[pause=1.0]

This slide lets us see how UNKNOWN behaves when combined with TRUE and FALSE.

[pause=0.7]

For example, TRUE AND UNKNOWN becomes UNKNOWN, because we do not know whether the missing side would have been true.

FALSE AND UNKNOWN becomes FALSE, because one false condition is already enough to make the entire AND expression false.

TRUE OR UNKNOWN becomes TRUE, because one true condition is enough.

[pause=0.8]

At the bottom, we have a runnable example that creates combinations of TRUE, FALSE, and UNKNOWN.

Run it in the browser and inspect the output table.

[pause=0.5]

If you want to study the behavior more closely, copy the query into pgAdmin and run it there.

You do not need to memorize every combination immediately. Focus on understanding why SQL sometimes cannot make a definite decision.

[pause=1.0]

Here we make the behavior of WHERE very clear.

[pause=0.7]

We create three sample rows: one with TRUE, one with FALSE, and one with UNKNOWN.

[pause=0.4]

Then we use the Boolean field directly in the WHERE clause.

[pause=0.7]

Before running the example, predict what will happen.

Only the TRUE row will remain. FALSE is removed, and UNKNOWN is also removed.

[pause=0.8]

Click Run in the browser to confirm this.

[pause=0.5]

You can copy the same SQL into pgAdmin if you want to experiment. For example, you could change the values or add another row.

This small example is important because later, when null appears in a comparison, the result may become UNKNOWN and disappear from your query even though you did not explicitly ask SQL to remove it.

[pause=1.0]

A very common beginner mistake is trying to compare a value to null using the equals operator.

[pause=0.7]

For example, writing email address equals null does not test whether the email is missing.

The result is UNKNOWN.

The same problem happens with not equal to null.

To test for missing data, SQL provides special predicates: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL.

[pause=0.8]

The code on this slide intentionally demonstrates the incorrect comparison so you can see what PostgreSQL returns.

Run it in the browser and look at the equals-null and not-equals-null columns.

You can also copy the code into pgAdmin.

[pause=0.7]

The rule to remember is simple: when checking whether a value is missing, use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. Do not use ordinary equals or not-equals comparisons.

[pause=1.0]

Missing text and blank text are not the same thing.

[pause=0.7]

A null value means the value is missing or unknown.

An empty string means we have text, but its length is zero.

We can also have text containing only spaces.

In real datasets, all three situations can appear.

A useful pattern is to first trim spaces using B trim, and then use null if to convert an empty result into null.

[pause=0.8]

The query on this slide finds email addresses that are either missing or effectively blank.

Run it directly in the browser and inspect the records it finds.

You can also copy the SQL to pgAdmin and run it there.

This kind of normalization is very useful before we start making decisions about whether a contact value is usable.

[pause=1.0]

Boolean columns can also contain null.

[pause=0.7]

Suppose consent to contact is a Boolean field.

TRUE can mean the person explicitly said yes.

FALSE can mean the person explicitly said no.

But null may mean that the answer was never recorded.

Those three states can have different business meanings.

PostgreSQL lets us test them explicitly using IS TRUE, IS FALSE, and IS UNKNOWN.

[pause=0.8]

Run the example in the browser and look at the three output columns. They clearly show which state each record belongs to.

[pause=0.5]

You can copy the query into pgAdmin as well.

[pause=0.7]

The main lesson is not to automatically treat FALSE and UNKNOWN as the same thing. In many applications, “no” and “we do not know” should lead to different actions.

[pause=1.0]

Ordinary equality and inequality comparisons can produce UNKNOWN when null is involved.

[pause=0.7]

PostgreSQL provides a useful alternative called IS DISTINCT FROM.

You can think of this as a null-safe comparison.

IS DISTINCT FROM tells us whether two values are different, even when one of them is null.

IS NOT DISTINCT FROM tells us whether two values match, including the case where both are null.

The useful part is that these comparisons return TRUE or FALSE rather than UNKNOWN.

[pause=0.8]

The SQL example compares bill amount with amount paid.

Run it in the browser and inspect the two comparison columns.

[pause=0.5]

You can also copy the query into pgAdmin and experiment with the values.

This operator becomes very useful when the business rule needs missing values to be handled explicitly.

[pause=1.0]

Now let's introduce coalesce.

[pause=0.7]

Coalesce returns the first value in a list that is not null.

For example, we might try an email address first. If that is missing, try the mobile phone. If that is also missing, try the home phone. Finally, we can return a readable fallback.

This is a very useful function, but we should use it carefully.

A fallback should have a real meaning. We do not want to replace missing data with a value that changes the meaning of the information.

In a few slides, we will combine coalesce with null if so that blank text is treated as missing before we choose the first usable contact method.

[pause=1.0]

Null if is another simple but useful SQL function.

[pause=0.7]

It compares two expressions. If they are equal, it returns null. Otherwise, it returns the first expression.

On this slide, we use B trim to remove spaces around an email address. Then null if converts an empty string into null.

This helps us normalize text before later logic.

[pause=0.8]

There is a runnable example below.

Click Run in the browser and compare the original email with the normalized email.

[pause=0.5]

Then, if you want to practice in PostgreSQL directly, click Copy, open pgAdmin, and run the query in the Query Tool.

Pay special attention to records containing blank or whitespace-only text. Those are the records where this pattern is most useful.

[pause=1.0]

Now we combine the previous two ideas.

[pause=0.7]

First, we clean each possible contact value. We trim extra spaces and convert blank values into null.

[pause=0.4]

Then we use coalesce to choose the first usable contact method.

The priority in this example is email first, then mobile phone, then home phone, and finally the text No contact provided.

[pause=0.8]

The SQL may look longer, but the logic is actually very systematic.

[pause=0.8]

Run the query in the browser and look at the preferred contact column.

[pause=0.4]

Then try copying it into pgAdmin.

As you read the expression, do not try to pronounce every parenthesis. Think about the workflow: clean email, clean mobile, clean home, and then choose the first value that is actually available.

[pause=1.0]

This example shows another use for null if.

[pause=0.7]

Suppose we want to calculate the percentage of a bill that has been paid.

Normally, we divide amount paid by bill amount.

But what happens if the bill amount is zero?

Division by zero causes a problem.

Here we use null if on the bill amount. If the denominator is zero, null if returns null instead. The result of the calculation then becomes null, which tells us the percentage is not computable.

[pause=0.8]

Run the SQL in the browser and inspect the percent paid column.

You can also copy it into pgAdmin.

Notice that null does not mean zero percent. It means we could not meaningfully calculate the ratio. That distinction is important when preparing data for analysis.

[pause=1.0]

Now we move to one of the most useful tools in this module: the case expression.

[pause=0.7]

Think of case as a sequence of questions.

SQL checks the first WHEN condition. If it is TRUE, SQL returns the corresponding THEN value and stops.

If it is not true, SQL moves to the next WHEN condition.

If none of the conditions match, SQL uses ELSE.

If there is no ELSE, the result becomes null.

[pause=0.7]

The most important phrase to remember is: first match wins.

That means the order of the branches matters.

Whenever you build a case expression, read the conditions from top to bottom and ask whether an earlier condition could accidentally capture records that were supposed to reach a later condition.

[pause=1.0]

This is called a searched case expression.

[pause=0.7]

Each WHEN contains a complete Boolean condition.

That makes searched case useful for ranges, null checks, and compound rules.

In this example, we classify billing amounts.

Missing amounts become Unknown. Amounts greater than or equal to ten thousand become High Value. Amounts greater than or equal to five thousand become Standard. Everything else becomes Low Value.

[pause=0.8]

We have the full SQL in the runnable code cell.

Click Run in the browser and compare the original bill amount with the new billing tier.

[pause=0.5]

You can also click Copy and run the same query in pgAdmin.

When reading this query, focus on the decision order rather than the punctuation. SQL is simply checking each rule from top to bottom and using the first rule that matches.

[pause=1.0]

There is another form called simple case.

[pause=0.7]

Simple case is useful when we are comparing one expression against several exact values.

Here, we start with payment status.

If the status is Paid, return Closed. If it is No Charge, also return Closed. If it is Open, return Follow up. If it is Pending Review, return Investigate. Otherwise, return Status missing.

[pause=0.8]

Run the query in the browser and compare the payment status with the action column.

[pause=0.5]

You can also copy the query into pgAdmin.

Compare this syntax with the searched case from the previous slide.

Use simple case when you are matching one value against a list of exact options. Use searched case when each branch needs its own full condition.

[pause=1.0]

This slide demonstrates one of the easiest case mistakes to make.

[pause=0.7]

In the first query, we check whether age is at least eighteen before checking whether age is at least sixty-five.

A sixty-five-year-old also satisfies the first condition, so SQL immediately labels that person Adult and never reaches the Senior branch.

That makes the Senior branch unreachable.

In the corrected version, we place the more specific condition first: age at least sixty-five, followed by age at least eighteen.

[pause=0.8]

Both versions are provided in the code cell.

Run them in the browser and compare the results.

You can also copy them into pgAdmin.

[pause=0.7]

Remember: when conditions overlap, put the more specific condition before the broader condition.

[pause=1.0]

When we create categories, exact boundaries need to be intentional.

[pause=0.7]

Here our billing rule begins with missing values.

[pause=0.4]

Then we handle amounts greater than or equal to ten thousand.

Next we handle amounts greater than or equal to five thousand.

Everything else goes into the low-value category.

If we add a special zero category, zero also needs to appear before the broad final ELSE branch.

When you design a rule like this, test the exact boundary values.

Try zero, five thousand, ten thousand, a value just below each threshold, and a null value.

A query that works for ordinary records may still contain a logic error at the boundaries, so boundary testing is an important part of validating SQL.

[pause=1.0]

An ELSE branch in a case expression is optional.

[pause=0.7]

If there is no ELSE and none of the WHEN conditions match, SQL returns null.

Sometimes that is exactly what we want.

But it should be a deliberate decision, not an accident.

In this example, only selected respiratory diagnoses receive the label Respiratory. Other diagnoses receive null because there is no ELSE branch.

[pause=0.8]

Run the SQL in the browser and inspect the diagnosis group column.

You can also copy it into pgAdmin.

[pause=0.4]

Then think about the purpose of the output. Would null be meaningful here, or would a label such as Other be easier for users to understand?

The answer depends on the business rule and how the result will be used.

[pause=1.0]

Let's collect several common mistakes in one place.

[pause=0.7]

First, mixing OR and AND without parentheses can change the meaning of the rule.

Second, comparing a field to null with equals does not work as a missing-value test.

Third, NOT IN becomes dangerous when the list itself contains null.

Fourth, ordinary not-equal comparisons can silently exclude records where the value is null.

[pause=0.5]

Finally, putting a broad case condition before a more specific condition can make the specific branch unreachable.

Notice that most of these queries are syntactically valid. PostgreSQL may run them without displaying an error.

That is why testing SQL is not only about asking whether the query runs. We also need to ask whether the result matches the intended rule.

[pause=1.0]

This is a classic SQL trap.

[pause=0.7]

The query asks for records whose payment status is not in a list containing Paid and null.

At first, that may look reasonable.

But a null inside the NOT IN list can cause comparisons that appear to be non-matches to become UNKNOWN.

The database cannot prove that a value is different from an unknown list element.

[pause=0.8]

Run the example in the browser and observe the result.

[pause=0.4]

Then copy it into pgAdmin if you want to test variations.

For example, remove null from the list and compare the output.

The safer approach is normally to keep null out of the list and handle missing values explicitly according to the business rule.

[pause=1.0]

Here we compare two different policies.

[pause=0.7]

The first query uses ordinary not equal to Paid.

If payment status is null, that comparison becomes UNKNOWN, so the row is filtered out.

The second query uses IS DISTINCT FROM Paid.

Now a missing status is treated as different from Paid and the record is included.

Run both queries in the browser and compare the results.

You should see one important difference caused by the null status.

You can also copy the queries into pgAdmin and run them separately.

Neither query is automatically the right query for every situation.

The correct choice depends on the question. Do we mean a status that is known and not Paid, or do we mean anything that is not definitely Paid?

[pause=1.0]

Now we start combining several ideas into a more realistic rule.

[pause=0.7]

We want active patients who explicitly consented to contact, have either Diabetes or Kidney Disease, and do not have a usable email address.

Notice how carefully the requirements are defined.

Active must be true.

Consent must explicitly be true. UNKNOWN consent is not treated as permission.

The diagnosis must be one of the target diagnoses.

[pause=0.5]

Finally, we normalize the email before checking whether it is missing.

[pause=0.8]

The full query is available in the code cell.

Run it in the browser and examine each returned record against the written rule.

[pause=0.5]

You can also copy the query into pgAdmin.

This is a good example of translating a real requirement into several small, testable SQL conditions.

[pause=1.0]

This example creates two useful outputs at the same time.

[pause=0.7]

First, we create a preferred contact method. We normalize blank values and use email, mobile phone, and home phone in that order.

Second, we create a billing category.

Notice that missing bill amounts become Needs review rather than being placed into the Low Value category.

An exact zero becomes No Charge.

[pause=0.4]

Then we apply the High Value and Standard thresholds.

[pause=0.8]

The SQL is available below.

Run it in the browser and study the preferred contact and billing tier columns.

[pause=0.5]

You can also use Copy and run it in pgAdmin.

[pause=0.7]

The important design idea is that presentation defaults should not hide data-quality problems. A missing bill is not the same thing as a small bill.

[pause=1.0]

Here we calculate length of stay.

[pause=0.7]

PostgreSQL allows us to subtract one date from another to get the number of days between them.

But first, we define the population.

We only want completed stays, so the WHERE clause removes records where the discharge date is null.

[pause=0.4]

Then the case expression categorizes the calculated stay.

Less than five days is Short. Five through ten days is Medium. More than ten days is Long.

Run the code in the browser and look at both the calculated number of days and the final category.

[pause=0.5]

You can also copy the query into pgAdmin.

This is a good example of separating two questions: first, which records belong in the analysis, and second, how should the included records be classified?

[pause=1.0]

Date-based rules can change every day if we always use the current system date.

[pause=0.7]

For teaching and reproducible analysis, sometimes we want a fixed reference date.

In this example, the reference date is August eleventh, twenty twenty-six.

We look at admissions in a thirty-day window and create a respiratory risk category.

[pause=0.8]

The query also joins admissions with patient information so we can use age in the rule.

Run the example here in the browser and inspect the admission dates and category.

You can copy it into pgAdmin as well.

Because the reference date is fixed, you and your classmates should get the same cohort even if you run the example on different days.

Later, in a production system, a dynamic date may be more appropriate.

[pause=1.0]

Most of the reasoning in this module transfers to other database systems.

[pause=0.7]

AND, OR, NOT, IS NULL, coalesce, null if, and case are widely supported concepts.

But some syntax varies across database systems.

For example, PostgreSQL supports IS DISTINCT FROM. Other database systems may handle null-safe comparison differently.

PostgreSQL can subtract one date from another directly. Another system may use a function such as date diff.

So when you move from PostgreSQL to another database, keep the logical rule the same, but check whether any syntax needs to change.

The best skill to carry between systems is not memorizing every command. It is being able to explain the rule clearly and then translate that rule into the target SQL dialect.

[pause=1.0]

Let's do a reasoning exercise before writing more SQL.

[pause=0.7]

We have two versions of a condition.

In Version A, age greater than or equal to sixty-five is connected by OR to a diagnosis-and-consent condition.

In Version B, age or diagnosis is grouped inside parentheses, and consent is required afterward.

Try to identify the patient who appears only when the parentheses are omitted.

A useful strategy is to look for an older patient whose consent is false.

Ask yourself: in Version A, does the consent condition apply to the age branch?

[pause=0.4]

Then compare that with Version B.

You can test the related query in the browser from the earlier slide, or copy it into pgAdmin and modify it yourself.

[pause=0.7]

The goal here is to explain why the results differ.

[pause=1.0]

Now let's practice text normalization and fallback values.

[pause=0.7]

The goal is to display a preferred language.

If the language contains useful text, keep it.

If it is null, empty, or only spaces, display Language not recorded.

The query first uses B trim and null if to normalize the text. Then coalesce provides the final fallback.

[pause=0.8]

Run the example in the browser and compare preferred language with language display.

[pause=0.5]

You can also click Copy and run the query in pgAdmin.

Try to identify which records actually needed the fallback.

This pattern is useful far beyond this example. Whenever user-entered text may contain blank or whitespace-only values, normalizing before applying business logic makes the result much more reliable.

[pause=1.0]

Here we improve our billing case expression by adding a special category for an exact zero.

[pause=0.7]

The order is important.

[pause=0.4]

First, check for null.

Second, check for zero and label it No Charge.

[pause=0.4]

Then check the High Value threshold.

After that, check the Standard threshold.

[pause=0.5]

Finally, use Low Value for the remaining known amounts.

[pause=0.8]

The complete query is available in the code cell.

Before running it, predict what will happen to zero, five thousand, ten thousand, and null.

[pause=0.4]

Then click Run in the browser and verify your predictions.

You can also copy the SQL into pgAdmin.

This is a good example of boundary testing. The exact values at the edges of categories deserve special attention.

[pause=1.0]

This practice asks a conceptual question.

[pause=0.7]

Why does the null-safe filter return one extra row?

The ordinary condition says payment status is not equal to Paid.

A null payment status cannot be proven to be different from Paid, so the comparison becomes UNKNOWN and the row is removed.

The null-safe version says payment status IS DISTINCT FROM Paid.

Now null can be included because PostgreSQL can make a definite true-or-false decision.

Look for the record with a missing payment status.

[pause=0.4]

Then decide which business question you actually mean.

Do you want records that are known to be something other than Paid?

Or do you want records that are not definitely Paid?

Those are different questions, and they require different SQL.

[pause=1.0]

For this practice, we change the fixed reference date.

[pause=0.7]

Instead of August eleventh, use August fifth, twenty twenty-six.

Before running the query, predict which admissions will move outside the thirty-day window.

This is a good exercise because it separates two different parts of the logic.

Changing the reference date changes which records are included in the cohort.

It does not change the rule that uses diagnosis and age to assign the risk category.

If you want, copy the earlier date query into pgAdmin and change only the reference date.

You can also make the same change in the browser code.

Try to change one part of the rule at a time. That makes it much easier to understand why the output changes.

[pause=1.0]

Now we are starting the coding exercises for Assignment 5.

[pause=0.7]

In Exercise 1, you need to return patients who are either age sixty-five or older, or have Kidney Disease, but explicit consent must apply to the entire rule.

The key idea is grouping.

Put the age and diagnosis alternatives inside parentheses. Then add the consent requirement with AND.

[pause=0.8]

You can write the SQL directly in the browser.

When you are ready, select Run and Check. The browser will test your answer.

Let's finish by reviewing the main ideas from Module 5.

[pause=0.7]

When AND and OR appear together, use parentheses to make the intended grouping clear.

Remember that SQL uses three logical states: TRUE, FALSE, and UNKNOWN.

Treat null values explicitly. Use IS NULL, Boolean predicates, and null-safe comparisons when the business rule requires them.

For text, normalize blank values before using fallbacks.

With case expressions, remember that the first true branch wins, so branch order matters.

And finally, test edge cases. Check null values, blanks, zero, exact thresholds, and overlapping conditions.

Throughout this module, you were able to run SQL directly in the browser, and you can also copy those same examples into pgAdmin for additional PostgreSQL practice.

The goal is not only to write SQL that runs. The goal is to write SQL that accurately represents the rule you intended.
